body_markdown:
Our[engineering culture](https://eng.wealthfront.com/2024/04/26/principles-of-engineering-culture-at-wealthfront/) at Wealthfront emphasizes Individual Ownership and Engineering participation throughout the Product Lifecycle. These are two things that make Wealthfront such an amazing place to work and grow as an engineer. Every new effort that we develop is owned by an individual project lead from Engineering; they are responsible for wholly owning the project and having a complete understanding of the work as it develops. Having one leading engineer ensures that things are always moving smoothly and are shipping in a timely manner, while never compromising the high-quality engineering and product standards that Wealthfront consistently maintains.


To highlight how and why we live these principles every day, let’s take a look at a recent example of a project that I led:[Wealthfront’s Custodial Accounts](https://www.wealthfront.com/529-custodial-accounts) . This was a fantastic exercise in project management for me as an engineer, and a strong example of how our product lifecycle processes enable us to move quickly and deliver value to our clients as often as possible.


**Product Decisions at Wealthfront**


Peers outside of Wealthfront often ask how product decisions are made here. In this industry, product decisions often happen upstream of engineering, without sufficient engineering input for important decisions. At Wealthfront, we involve engineers from the very beginning of project ideation so that engineering considerations are made from the very start. I’m always extremely excited to tell people about Wealthfront’s approach since we find it works much better for everyone involved.


The engineering project lead is empowered to be a key decision maker from the very start of the project. Before we even began to talk about Custodial Accounts, Wealthfront leaders made sure that I was included in the room to represent the engineering organization in every decision made. Doing this upfront enables us to strike a balance between reasonable technical complexity and the product requirements for projects. Also, involving project stakeholders in every important conversation makes sure that everyone is on the same page from the very beginning. This kind of clear communication allows everyone to work better and more efficiently together.


**Communicating as the Lead Engineer**


At Wealthfront, many inputs are needed from several teams beyond just engineering. Custodial Accounts involved engineers, product managers, designers, content writers, legal and compliance, marketing, product and operations specialists, and many others. People from each of these functions become stakeholders in the project who provide specialized inputs about their respective areas of expertise.


Likewise, the project lead makes sure that these stakeholders are aware of what’s going on in the project as a whole. If there are any roadblocks to resolve or coordination needed, the project lead lets every stakeholder know as soon and as often as possible. After all, we are all on the same team and are trying to solve the same problems, so no stakeholder or project lead needs to face project setbacks alone.


**What are we shipping, and when? And why?**


When building at Wealthfront, we want to ship high quality products while also moving as quickly as possible (for example,[deploying our changes straight to production](https://www.wealthfront.com/engineering) ). Engineering is the primary driver in setting timelines for our projects, and we strive to build high-quality systems quickly yet safely for our clients. Our product team saw a prime opportunity to release Custodial Accounts when they would provide the most benefit for our clients. Engineering was very involved in helping our product partners decide what we should build for this opportunity. Together, we settled on a short yet achievable timeline for engineering: only 6 weeks from breaking ground on the project to delivering something real for clients to use, while meeting all of our usual quality and safety standards that we ensure for all of our accounts.


We laid out incremental milestones to have something usable every 2 weeks, or every sprint for our team. We made these milestones well-defined with a complete list of included features so that the relevant users for each milestone would know exactly what to expect. After just one sprint, our team developed an internal functioning MVP (minimum viable product) with a subset of features that enabled a controlled group of our employees to open and fund new Custodial accounts, when just 2 weeks prior Wealthfront was not able to support this at all. With this barebones version of the account, Wealthfront employees already began to invest real money for their children.


This proof of concept gave the team early confidence that Custodial Accounts would work as expected, on the timeline we expected. The MVP also helped identify potential issues early instead of later in the project’s development, when issues are more difficult to fix.


During each of the following two-week sprints, we continued to ship milestones to clients beyond just employees. Building a functional MVP upfront gave us a strong technical base to continue to build off of and aligned the team in a unified direction for the best way to continue developing the product.


**My Takeaways (Presented as Cliche Sayings)**


As cliche as they might be, I love living by a number of different sayings, metaphors, and anything in between. After all, they’re cliche because people over-use them, and people probably over-use them because of how true they are.


1. **Measure Twice, Cut Once**
Good planning, foresight, and contingencies can always make up for issues that come up later. However, nothing down the line can compensate for poor planning because poor planning will guarantee that the quality of the project suffers. Any effort spent planning upfront pays for itself several times over in the amount of ease that it introduces to the project later.
2. **Move fast! But don’t break things.**
The faster we ship projects, the sooner that clients start getting more value out of Wealthfront. However, our clients deeply trust us with their finances (you can read my thoughts on trust and Wealthfront[here](https://eng.wealthfront.com/2026/08/03/7-words-7-journeys-the-wealthfront-new-college-grad-experience/) ), and breaking parts of the Wealthfront experience would be a disservice to the trust that we’ve built with clients over many years. Wealthfront is extremely diligent in our risk controls and upholding strong compliance standards that protect our clients and their assets. We always want to deliver value to clients as often as possible, but it will never be done with shortcuts at the expense of quality or client safety.
3. **Communicate Up, Down, and Sideways**
In any project, any number of things can and will go wrong. The best thing to do is always to communicate bumps in the road as soon and as far as possible. Getting everyone on the same page allows everyone to help get the collective back on track and to help everyone make decisions with complete information.


Today, Custodial accounts are empowering Wealthfront clients to invest for their children every day. Seeing these accounts is genuinely an awesome reminder for me about how Wealthfront’s intentional processes empowered us to efficiently deliver a great product for our clients. It is also a powerful testament to the strong quality of work and the quality of the individuals at Wealthfront who I am excited to work with every day.
